title: Native Signers in Place-Name Deed Records
summary: Many place-name studies preserve Indigenous land names through colonial deed language, but the people named in those same records can be easy to miss. The records gathered here show cases where a placename, deed boundary, treaty, or confirmation also names Native signers, sachems, witnesses, interpreters, or representatives. Nearby leaders are included only when the cited record names them.
content:
Why Signers Matter

Western Long Island Records

  • Marossepinck, Rockaway, Sint Sinck, and Secatogue boundary language, 1639: A January 15, 1639 Dutch deed names Mechowodt or Mechoswodt, chief sachem of Marossepinck, with Piscamoc/Pisacome, Wattewochkeouw, Kachpoher, and Ketchquawars as co-owners. The deed's broad boundary language reached from Rockaway toward Sicketeuwhacky/Secatogue and north toward Garritsen's Bay. [2. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV.; Sandi Brewster-Walker research document dated April 19, 2017.]
  • Hempstead Plains, Merrick/Merriack, Massapequa, and Rockaway, 1643: The Hempstead deed references names Tackapousha with Aarane or Jorrane, Pamaman, Remoj or Remos, Waines or Wamis, Whanage or Whanege, and Yarafus or Gerasco. The sources connect the record collectively with Massapequa, Merrick/Merriack, and Rockaway representation, but do not safely assign every listed person to one modern community label. [3. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911).; John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV.; Sandi Brewster-Walker research document dated April 19, 2017.]
  • Rockaway Neck, 1655: The Rockaway Neck deed context names Ruckquaheag, Ronnessoke or Suscaneman, Adam/Achitteronose, and eight unnamed people. Adam is important because related records describe him as bilingual and as an intermediary; the history treats him as a signer and possible interpreter only where the cited record supports that reading. [4. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.]
  • Western Long Island treaty, 1656: A March 12, 1656 agreement names Waghtummoore, Wogquatis, Uppahanuum, Tackapousha, Adam, and Rumegie. The alliance represented communities including Secatogue, Maskinekaug/Matinecock, Merrick, Rockaway, and Canarsie. [5. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV.]
  • Hempstead conference, 1657: Strong names Tackapousha, Mangwobe of Rockaway, Wyandanch, Cockenoe, and Merrick village representatives in a meeting with Hempstead officials. Cockenoe is identified in the references as Wyandanch's advisor and interpreter. [6. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.]
  • Massapeoque Meadows, 1658: A Massapequa references preserves signers including Tackapousha, Chopeyconnows/Chopeyconnaws, Sashamosse of Rockaway, Mattacaman, Manockeamicoke of Secatogue, Wow-house, Ramerock Drummer, and John Smith. [7. An Illustrated History of Massapequa.]
  • Jamaica confirmation, 1662: Strong's notes on Jamaica records mention Waumitumpacke and associates in an April 15, 1662 confirmation context. [8. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.; Records of Jamaica.]

Setauket And Cataconacke Records

  • Setauket, 1655: Strong and Setauket references identify Warawakmy, a Setauket sachem, in the April 14, 1655 deed. Additional references connect John Mahue and Massetuse with the record trail, while Strong emphasizes that Wyandanch is not named in that 1655 Setauket deed. [9. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.; Setauket 1655-1955: The First Three Hundred Years.; John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011).]
  • Cataconacke / Old Field, 1659: Strong describes John Mahue negotiating over Cataconacke with Wyandanch and advisors Checonow/Cockenoe and Sasarataicko/Sassakataka. A 1667 deposition records that Wyandanch appointed Sakkatakka and Chekanno to mark the tract. It identifies Pauquatoun—not Sasarataicko—as the former chief counselor. [10. John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011), p. 51; Gaynell Stone, ed., The History and Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), p. 199.]

Handling Uncertainty

Wyandanch, Cockenoe, Tackapousha, Adam/Achitteronose, and other leaders were active across many overlapping diplomatic networks. The history includes them in a placename moment only when a cited deed, conference, treaty, or source discussion names them in that record. When a person may have been alive, nearby, related, or politically relevant but is not named in the source, that context belongs in a biography or separate source discussion, not as a placename signer claim.
why_this_matters: Placenames become clearer when read alongside the Native people named in deed records, without unsupported guesses about who signed, translated, or represented a community.
activity_update_summary: Corrected the Cataconacke signer entry with exact pages, clarified the chief-counselor wording, and linked Sasarataicko's biography.
